articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s Pool Advisory Committee held its first meeting on Monday, July 12. Five residents were appointed to the committee on March 29. They include David del Villar Fernandez, Sarah Olsen Meyjes, Carolyn Pan, Steve Roland, and Lynne Wright. City Councilmember Betsy Andersen serves as the Council Liaison. Recreation Director Chelle Putzer serves as staff liaison. Also in attendance were Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Sustainability Manager Alyssa Dykman, and Special Assistant to City Administrator Paul Benoit. Also present were representatives from Griffin Structures, to include project manager George Sanen. City Council unanimously approved an agreement with Griffin Structures as the project manager on June 7, noting the firm’s extensive portfolio in aquatic design throughout the state. A contract of $612,700, which includes a 10% contingency, was awarded. Sanen has more than 30 years of experience in program and construction management of multi-million dollar recreational, aquatic, and community centers. The committee’s task is to offer advice based on each member’s skill-set and expertise throughout the design process of the project. Members will also serve as a conduit for the community in the design refinement and construction of the Piedmont Community Pool, made possible through a $19.5 million bond that voters approved in November 2020. Councilmember Andersen extended her thanks to the community for approving the measure. Although the committee is ad-hoc and will meet when needed throughout the design process, Roland, the committee chair, said that members should be prepared to meet “possibly twice a week” as early as next Spring. articles.text: Woodminster Summer Musicals, an open-air amphitheater located in Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland hills, has reopened with Always, Patsy Cline with shows this Friday and Sunday, July 16 and 18, and two the following weekend, July 23 and 25. The play was created and originally directed by Ted Swindley and is based the true story of the titular character Cline, born Virginia Patterson Hensley in 1932. The country-pop superstar died at age 30 in a 1963 plane crash at the height of her career, but in her short life has become considered one of the most influential, successful, and acclaimed vocalists of the 20th century. The play highlights the relationship between her and Houston housewife Louise Seger, who became an avid fan of Cline’s. The two women struck up a friendship that culminated in Cline spending the night at Seger’s house - where the narrative of “Always, Patsy Cline” begins. Margaret Belton stars as Patsy Cline, and Julia Etzel is Louise Seger. The show is directed by Joel Schlader, son of Woodminster founders Harriet and Jim Schlader. Tickets for the show can be purchased at woodminster.com, or by calling the box office at (510) 531-9597. Tickets must be purchased in advance. All shows begin at 8 p.m. Woodminster Amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland hills.

articles.text: Editor: An issue has arisen in our neighborhood that seems a bit symptomatic of the dissension and maybe even hatred that is prevalent in our country today. Our neighbors came to our door, angry and offended. Why? Because we had hanging for the first time a “thin blue line” flag in support of our police, who have over 27 years personally ensured the safety of our family and have kept our city a place of peace. It seems our neighbors do not see this flag as a symbol of appreciation and endorsement of Piedmont Police, but instead as an emblem of white supremacy. We were stunned, as this was a new take on the meaning of the flag to us, but they were adamant that if we did research, we’d see that they were right. So, we did some research, finding that its original meaning is to honor men and women who dedicate their lives to keeping the public safe. We also spoke to our friend, a captain in the Oakland Police Department and to a Piedmont Police officer. But our neighbors were right that the “thin blue line” flag has been reimagined by some to represent racism, and there is a narrative that somehow the police flag represents white supremacy, even though the police across the country and in our community are multiracial themselves. Reportedly, some bigots at Charlottesville carried the flag, giving rise to the white supremacy theory. So which narrative to accept? What is the right, which perception to believe? After our research and various discussions seeking alternate points of view, we have come to a decision. Our choice is to accept the original, positive meaning of the “thin blue line” flag and to reject the negative, divisive version, not buying into any form of hate. We hope that our neighbors respect our honest and freedom of choice and not disbelieve our intent, which is simply to show gratitude and support to the Piedmont Police Department. articles.text: • The City of Piedmont maintains an exclusive Franchise Agreement with Republic Services to provide solid waste, recycling, and organic collection services in the city. New service rates became effective July 1, 2021. Are you wondering how to save money on your household’s garbage collection services? Here are a couple of ways to reduce the cost: • The Annual Pre-Payment Discount allows single family customers to voluntarily pay for one (1) year of service with the twelfth (12th) month of service provided at no charge. That is 12 months of service for the cost of 11 months of service. Enroll in the discount by contacting Republic Services. • Service rates are based upon the size of your garbage cart. Collection service for recyclables and organics is unlimited in volume and provided at no additional cost. By recycling more and generating less garbage, you may be able to switch to a smaller garbage cart to save money. But be sure to choose the right container for your garbage needs. Charges will be assessed for overflowing garbage, garbage set out beyond your service level, or allowing garbage to accumulate on your property. Recycling carts and organics carts contaminated with garbage will not be serviced. Call Republic Services at (800) 320-8077 to order additional or larger carts for recyclables and organics. • On-premises (backyard) collection service costs more than curbside service. Switching to curbside service saves approximately $46 per month. With curbside collection, the customer is responsible for placing the wheeled carts at the curb on their regular collection service day and returning the carts to their storage location promptly after collection. With curbside collection, carts are not limited in size as they are with on-premises collection. Physically disabled residential customers with no able-bodied household members are eligible to receive on-premises (backyard) collection at curbside rates. The maximum cart size available to on-premises collection is 35 gallons. To receive the discount, the account holder must fill out the application for exemption to curbside placement of carts, provide a doctor’s certification that the customer is unable to move the carts to the curb or provide a copy of a valid California Disability Placard, and verify that there are no able-bodied household members that can move the carts to the curb. Republic Services can be contacted about these services via phone (800-320-8077), email (piedmont@republicservices. com), or online at https://www. republicservices.com/municipality/piedmont-ca. To learn more about Piedmont Evergreen, the City of Piedmont’s outreach and education program for waste reduction, recycling, and composting, visit the City’s website: https://piedmont.ca.gov. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager “Your brilliant new sales manager had just one brilliant idea.”

articles.text: Highest rates of infection in areas with lowest vaccine rates According to the Alameda County Public Health Office, COVID cases have more than doubled in the county since early June, threatening to “exceed the Spring wave” experienced earlier this year. In early June, cases and hospitalizations were at their lowest levels since April 2020, the onset of the pandemic. The agency attributes the latest increases to reopened activities along with decreasing mask use. A small number of “generally mild cases” are reported among vaccinated individuals, but the vast majority of new cases are in those who are unvaccinated, County Health Officer Nicholas Moss explained. “We expect to see more COVID-19 with reopening, but the rate of this increase is concerning,” Moss said. “COVID-19 is a serious threat to the health and wellness of unvaccinated residents. If you are still deciding about vaccination, continue to follow COVID safety precautions to keep from catching or spreading the virus, like wearing your mask in indoor public settings and outdoor crowded spaces. If you are experiencing COVID-19 symptoms, please get tested, and if you’re positive, stay home until you have completed your isolation.” The agency is urging residents who are unvaccinated to seek out opportunities available for them, either through the county or healthcare provider. The Alameda County Health Care Services Agency issued a $12 million Request for Proposal (RFP) last month to support the outreach and operation of hyperlocal vaccination sites. “Talk to your friends, family members, religious leaders, or health care providers today. Ask your questions and get the information you need to make the decision that is right for you. When you are ready, we’ll be ready for you and in your neighborhood,” said Dr. Jocelyn Freeman Garrick, Alameda County’s lead for COVID-19 vaccinations and testing. “Vaccine is free for everyone 12 and up and all currently available vaccines are recommended by medical professionals because they are effective. You don’t need insurance and you won’t be asked for your immigration status.” Delta variant causes concern Dr. George Rutherford, UCSF Professor of Epidemiology and Piedmont resident, joined a UCSF “Grand Rounds” panel of medical professionals last month to discuss the emerging Delta variant and covid developments globally. Rutherford explained that the Delta variant, one of the two variants to emerge from India, could account for as many as 70% of cases in California by the end of the summer. The variant is agreed to be more transmissible; however, mRNA vaccines appear to be effective against the Delta variant. articles.text: A Gubernatorial Recall Election will be held on September 14 within the state of California to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom from office. The Alameda County Registrar of Voters released a press release on July 9 announcing the recall election. The nomination period for the recall election was held July 9 through July 16. A recall procedure has been part of the state’s political system since 1911 and provides a mechanism for the public to attempt to remove elective public officials from office before the end of their term. At least 1,495,000 valid petition signatures, or 12% of the votes cast for the office of Governor in 2018, were received. Democrat Gov. Newsom is the second California governor ever to face a recall election. Five attempts to recall the governor have failed to qualify for the ballot since he took office in January 2019. Gray Davis was removed from office in 2003, only the second state governor successfully recalled in U.S. history. He was replaced by actor Arnold Schwarzenegger. All active registered voters in California will automatically receive a mail ballot for the recall election.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department offers dozens of fun summer courses, classes, camps and sports leagues, but the most fun has been the Creative Drama camp for 5-9 year olds operated by Fool Moon Theatre Arts. Program director Jesse Vail brings out the inner thespian in every young actor by teaching a little theater skills and having a whole lot of fun. The class is a two-week crash course in puppetry, miming, clowning, improv, and role playing to prepare young jesters, actresses, and playwrights for a one-hour variety show called Clown Extravaganza for the entertainment of family and friends on the final day of the camp. The Post had the opportunity to peek in on their performance last Friday, July 9. The show started off by immediately taking down the 4th wall in a piece called “Wee at the Theater.” The clowns lined up in a row with popcorn in tow and watched a movie, but the screen was an audience of smiling and filming parents. A comical game of “telephone” ensued. The campers performed a variety of skits for an hour, replete with dance moves, costumes, songs, and music without a cue card in sight. In the skit “As Fire as the Eye Can See,” a blind firefighter tries to locate a clown on “fire.” Another crowd favorite “Pie 5” found the clown Bongo, The Recreation Department’s Creative Drama troupe cheers at the end of the skit “Wee at the Theater.” Isla Day (right) laughs as Bongo the Clown, played by Natasha Weinstein, puts a pie in her own face. Behind the scenes, clowns prepare the props for the next skit and await their cue from ringleader Jesse Vail. Vail, who has taught the course for 10 years, runs his own theater production company. He also teaches stagecraft at Piedmont High. He inherited the theater program at the Rec. Department from Randy McCommons when he retired from the department after 30 years. “I met with Randy before I took it over, because he wanted to give me the philosophy behind this class and that is ‘the creative act.’ It is not just writing stuff and putting kids on stage, but having them create and work together,” Vail said. “Because this is creative drama I give them certain challenges to create some of their own content,” Vail said. ”The best part of the creative drama camps is the [kids] get to say what they want to do and help make it happen. They design their own costumes and make their own props,” said camp assistant Madi Chicas. articles.text: Magical thinking in the modern world My five-year-old lost her first tooth yesterday and she was so excited. She came bounding into my room, showed me the tooth and asked, “Will you text the tooth fairy, so she knows about my tooth?” “Of course!” I replied, carefully getting out my phone and starting to very rapidly “text” without her seeing the screen. When I was a kid, the tooth fairy was very real to me. I had a powerful imagination and I used it to help conjure up all sorts of magical creatures in my life. Moreover, each of those imaginative characters was part of a narrative. Put all of those narratives together and I lived in a world where I had friends, both real and imaginary, and special moments that had magical components to them, both real and imaginary. Kids need those narratives to help make sense of their world. Why do we need unicorns and dragons? Maybe to prove that there are powerful forces of good that can defend us from the unknown or that which we can’t control? Why do kids love Santa, the Tooth Fairy, the Easter Bunny? Maybe to remind us that ritual and tradition are a way to organize the passing of time and the marking of moments. The more our young kids play with magical thinking, the stronger their imaginations will grow. The more that we as parents can create the space and structure for our children to explore their imaginative play, the more that kind of play can thrive in our homes. The kids will do all the hard work...their brains will create the friends, the magical creatures and the associated stories. Your job is to listen, be curious and give space for their ideas to flourish. But what struck me as my daughter asked me to text the tooth fairy is that her world of “real” is so different from the one in which I grew up. Today, we are constantly connected with each other – and we don’t even have to worry about long distance phone calls. All information is at our fingertips without even learning the Dewey decimal system. Our kids have grown up with all of these devices and technologies at their fingertips. I am so excited to think about how we can support the amazing imaginations of our children and the incredible benefits of magical thinking in their early years and, simultaneously, honor the real world that we live in right now. The next time you hear your child talking about the monster under the bed, the fairy who lives in your backyard, the unicorn that comes to visit her when she’s playing outside, take advantage of our digital culture. Supporting your child’s imaginative journey with the tools of the real world can be fun for both parent and child. Email that imaginary friend, design a dragon on a drawing app, ask the unicorn what it wants to order from Uber Eats, and text the Tooth Fairy! Nina Meehan is CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. Whitney, America’s highest peak at 14,202 feet, Piedmont Scouts in Troop arrived at the Whitney Portal, elevation approximately 8,000 feet, on Monday afternoon, June 14, after a 7-hour drive from Piedmont. On Tuesday, the Troop went for a 7-mile warm up hike in the Horseshoe Meadow area around 10,000 to 11,000 feet elevation to acclimate. On Wednesday, June 16, the Troop began its expedition from Whitney Portal to Trail Camp at elevation 12,000’, with approximately a 4,000’ elevation gain over seven miles of rough terrain. The next day, Thursday, the Scouts arose at 3 a.m. to climb the eastern face of the Whitney circ. Miguel Long and Henry Smith were the first to reach the summit at 6:10 a.m., followed by Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill, Paul Jahn, Peter Ashton and William Campbell. The entire team summited by 8 a.m. One hour later everyone had to turn around and descend due to forecasts of lightening. Everyone returned to Trail Camp at 12,000 with weather conditions deteriorating and massive thunder clouds building in the Whitney Circ. The Trail Master made the safety call for the team to move to a lower position and the team hiked another 3.5 miles and 2,000’ lower. After a bit of rest and watching expert angler Miguel Long snag a Golden Trout from a stream, the Scouts enjoyed a gourmet meal of freeze-dried cuisine and scoops of peanut butter. Throughout the night the conditions worsened, and the thunder roiled among the granite walls. Rain dumped from the skies. A wildfire started at the bottom of the Whitney Portal Canyon created a red glow in the cloudy night sky. After a 7 a.m. wake-up call, the Scouts team departed for the remaining 4-mile descent of 2000 feet to the Whitney Portal trailhead. Each list covers a handful of selections in genres or categories such as Romance, Historical Fiction, Audio Books, and Thrillers. This assemblage spans the genre of “Thrillers” with books covering every shade of drama and intrigue, including murders, ghosts, psychological thrillers, legal disputes and domestic dramas. The descriptions and reviews have been edited for length. The Secret Talker, by Geling Yan (HarperVia, 150 pp.) There are no gun-fueled bloodbaths, global conspiracies or triple-crossing operatives in The Secret Talker, a book written by the well-known Chinese author Geling Yan, that describes the turbulent mysteries of the heart. An uncannily perceptive stranger strikes up an email correspondence with Hongmei, a Chinese transplant living in California. Hongmei resists, then plunges headlong into an ever more personal email correspondence with her mysterious interlocutor. The anonymity of the conversation allows the protagonist to share distressing secrets – details of her early life in China, including her interrogation and imprisonment, her move to America, and the disappointments of her marriage. Just 150 pages long, The Secret Talker is a profound meditation on love, the difficulties of communication and the agonizing joy and brutality of commitment. The Quiet Boy, by Ben H. Winters (Mulholland Books, 448 pp.) Winters’ novel first appears to be a conventional well-written and punchy legal thriller set in our own world — until it turns out to be something else. It begins when Jay Shenk, a lawyer who has made ambulance-chasing into a high art, is alerted to what seems to be a sure thing as a medical malpractice case. Something has gone wrong with a teenager named Wesley Keener, who had routine surgery to relieve the pressure in his brain after hitting his head. The book then jumps forward a decade to 2019 when Shenk is a disappointed, haunted man, crushed by the derailment of the earlier lawsuit. The story emerges in expertly paced scenes moving backward and forward between present and past. Winters is such a fine writer that by the time he asks you to suspend your disbelief, you’ll follow him anywhere. The Drowning Kind, by Jennifer McMahon (Scout Press, 320 pp.) The most memorable character in Jennifer McMahon’s haunting tale is the water in Brandenburg Springs, Vermont, which grants wishes and heals ailments. It also has a habit of killing people. As the book Author Bryan Christy, previously an investigative reporter for National Geographic, wrote In the Company of Killers in which an investigative journalist travels to South Africa on his most dangerous assignment yet. begins, Jackie, a social worker, is heading home to Vermont. The body of her beloved but mentally unstable sister, Lexie, has just been found floating, face down, in the family’s springfed swimming pool. Jackie finds notebooks full of Lexie’s increasingly unhinged musings about their family history and the properties of the pool, which seems either bottomless or to change depths daily. Cut to a parallel story set in 1929, when a nervous, superstitious young bride travels with her husband to the newly opened Brandenburg Springs Hotel and Resort. They’re desperate for a baby, and they hear that the springs have unusual life-restoring properties. An uncannily perceptive stranger strikes up an email correspondence with Hongmei, a Chinese transplant living in California. Hongmei resists, then plunges headlong into an ever more personal email correspondence with her mysterious interlocutor. The anonymity of the conversation allows the protagonist to share distressing secrets – details of her early life in China, including her interrogation and imprisonment, her move to America, and the disappointments of her marriage. Just 150 pages long, The Secret Talker is a profound meditation on love, the difficulties of communication and the agonizing joy and brutality of commitment. The Quiet Boy, by Ben H. Winters (Mulholland Books, 448 pp.) Winters’ novel first appears to be a conventional well-written and punchy legal thriller set in our own world — until it turns out to be something else. It begins when Jay Shenk, a lawyer who has made ambulance-chasing into a high art, is alerted to what seems to be a sure thing as a medical malpractice case. Something has gone wrong with a teenager named Wesley Keener, who had routine surgery to relieve the pressure in his brain after hitting his head. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. articles.text: America’s Kuss wins Stage 15; Cavendish wins his 34th Grand Tour stage Photos courtesy of CyclingNews.com Tadej Pogacar has held the yellow jersey since Stage 8. He’s expected to defend his title with strong performances this week. Heading into the final week of racing, defending champion Croatian rider Tadej Pogacar holds the yellow jersey with a five-minute, 18-second advantage in the general classification standings over Rigoberto Uran. England’s Mark Cavendish tied the record of cycling legend Eddie Merckx after winning his 34th stage race at the Tour de France. His victory in Stage 13 on July 9 tied Merckx’s record. Cavendish will have his best opportunities to claim the record as his own come on the final three days of the tour: Stage 19’s flat course on July 16 from Mourenx to Libourne, Stage 20’s time trial from Libourne to Saint-Emilion on July 17, and the finale on the Champs-Élysées in Paris on July 18. Stage 15 was a big day for the United States when American Sepp Kuss, riding with Team Jumbo-Bisma, won the 191.3 kilometer mountain course, tossing his sunglasses into the crowd, raising his hands in victory into the air before covering his face with emotion. Kuss became the first American rider to win a stage at the Grand Tour since Tyler Farrar in 2011. The Tour looks ahead to a pair of mountain stages in Stage 17 today, Wednesday, July 14, and England’s Mark Cavendish tied Eddie Merckx with 34 overall Tour de France stage wins and four victories in this year’s race.

Wednesday, July 14, 2021 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 14th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. Piedmont High Class of 2021 Smith College Class of 2025 Sadie Tschider heads to Smith College in Massachusetts after becoming Piedmont High girls’ lacrosse program’s all-time leading assister as a four-year starter. The team finished 6-4 this year and was 2-2 when the pandemic struck last year. It was 20-2 when they won the NCS Championship in her sophomore year, and 14-11 as a freshman. She was named Sophomore of the Year by the Post in 2019 and was an honorable mention selection as Freshman of the Year in 2018. Tschider logged a team-leading 29 assists in 2021, 16 in four 2020 appearances, a school-record 66 as a sophomore, and 21 as a freshman. Below she details her workout regimen ahead of heading east this fall. What is your workout program this summer? I do a combination of strength training, high intensity intervals, and agility. Additionally, I have stickwork and ground ball routines that I do to maintain my technique. I do some workouts directly from Smith College Strength and Conditioning and add in my own routines as well. What are your fitness goals for this summer? This summer I have been working on my mile time, short sprint times and decreasing my time on my stickwork tests. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development by repeating workouts and consistently timing different running tests. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work with a trainer on my strength and agility. I also have been coaching younger lacrosse players, which helps me to maintain my stick skills, lacrosse IQ, and footwork. I love playing with the players that I coach; they always teach me as I am teaching them. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Photo by Todd Marshburn I am really proud of staying consistent with my training this summer. I am working out five days a week and doing stick-work at least three days a week. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? My advice is to put the time into the things you love. Hard work and effort will always win over natural talent. It is also important to have fulfilling hobbies, spend time on academics and enjoy time with the people you love. MICHAEL AIKAWA Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2023 Michael Aikawa was our 2021 Sophomore of the Year after carrying a .396 batting average last season on the baseball team. He had a team-leading .625 slugging percentage, .547 on-base percentage, and 1.172 on-base plus slugging percentage out of the leadoff spot; smacking two home runs, 20 runs scored, 13 RBIs, three doubles, and one triple. Aikawa, the second baseman, had two game-winning hits in Piedmont’s 12-4 season. Against St. Joseph on April 3, he hit a monumental two-run homer in the bottom of the sixth against to win 6-5. On March 20 versus Oakland Tech, Aikawa cracked a one run, one-out double in bottom of the fifth to snap a 0-0 deadlock in their 2-0 win over the Bulldogs. What is your workout program this summer? I am playing baseball every day and spent several weeks in Arizona at national tournaments. When I have off days, I have a workout program to help increase my strength, explosiveness, and speed. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I want to continue getting stronger and faster. I am hoping to lower my 30- and 60-yard dash times, increase my range for fielding, and be generally more explosive to the ball. How are you measuring your development? For strength, being able to increase my repetitions and increase the amount of weight. For speed, I get timed in game and feel more burst when stealing bases. It’s a little harder to measure my explosiveness, but my bat speed and drive to the ball seem to be progressing. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work with my college development team coach, a trainer, with my friends and teammates, and on my own. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I am now the leadoff hitter and starting shortstop for my college development team. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Manage your time, study hard, and put in the extra time. It will all pay off if you work hard on your craft. Photo by Todd Marshburn Emily Fitzgerald will be a junior this year. She’s a versatile forward leading coach Dan Chubbock’s attack. SADIE TSCHIDER Lacrosse EMILY FITZGERALD Soccer Piedmont High Class of 2023 Emily Fitzgerald enters her junior year at Piedmont High as a critical player on the soccer team as a striker and central attacking midfielder. She has been a starter since her freshman year in 2020. The Highlanders finished 4-1-5 last season and 7-5-7 in her freshman season. In February 2020, she scored the game-winning goal in the NCS Opening Round 2-1 win over No. 5 Urban while on the road in San Francisco as the No. 12 seeded team. PHS then beat No. 4 Lick 1-0 in the quarterfinals to reach its fourth consecutive NCS Semifinals. which they lost to the No. 1 seed, Cardinal Newman. What is your workout program this summer? I have practice with my club team, The Rage, four times a week, which has some strength training. I also do technical trainings on my own about 2-3 times a week. I try to swim at least three times a week as well. It’s super important that I stretch and roll out my muscles every day to prevent injury. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goal for this summer is to become stronger by lifting weights. I also want to maintain or increase my stamina in order to play 90 minutes of soccer with minimal fatigue. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development using films of my games to look for ways to improve. With film, I can notice what I did well and what I need to work on. With each game, I am able to see improvement. Something that also helps measure my development is feedback from coaches and college recruiters. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Outside of training with my club, I work with trainer, coach, and soccer professional Nikolai Littleton (a Piedmont grad), who focuses on my technical skills and strength training. I also train with other Piedmont High students. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I recently just played in the ECNL playoffs in Florida, which was a great experience and amazing for college exposure. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? The advice I would give is to work hard, and don’t let setbacks stop you from going after your goals. Listen to your mind and body to stay healthy. Most importantly, enjoy the game and have fun. articles.text: The CONCACAF Gold Cup is rolling through its first of three Group Stage matches. The U.S. Men’s National Team opened with an unconvincing 1-0 win over Haiti on Sunday, July 11 in Kansas City, and next will play low-ranked Martinique on Thursday, July 15. They close the Group stage with current Group B leader, Canada, on Sunday, July 18. The early U.S. goal was scored in the 8th minute after Shaquell Moore sent a hard pass to Gyasi Zardes, who flicked a looping pass above the defense to Sam Vines for a header goal. But that was it for the scoring. While U.S. manager Gregg Berhalter’s bunch did well to own 63 percent time of possession and have 13 total shots with five on target, Haiti had 10 shots, three on target, and created several chances. The United States looks ahead to non-FIFA member Martinique, which recently lost 4-1 to Canada. In the end, Group B is building toward a major meeting between USA and Canada on Sunday at 2:00 p.m. It will likely determine the top seed of the group, and the U.S.’s neighbors to the north aren’t anyone to take lightly. Although they are without wingback Alphonso Davies and striker Jonathan David, the Canadians last beat Haiti 3-0 in their World Cup Qualifiers on June 15. Group B brings a favorable route to the finals; the winner Photos courtesy of CONCACAF.com Sam Vines scored a goal in the 8th minute in a 1-0 win over Haiti on July 11. moves on to play the runner up of Group C in the quarterfinals on July 29, likely Costa Rica or Jamaica. For the semifinals, the Group B quarterfinal winner will face either Honduras, Panama, or Qatar from Group D, with El Salvador from Group A as a possibility. If the U.S. finishes as No. 2 in Group B, things become much more difficult. They would still face Costa Rica or Jamaica in the quarterfinals, but likely meet the tournament favorites, Mexico, in the semifinals. The U.S. team roster included 19 players from Major League Soccer, the U.S. professional league, and was without many U.S. players currently under contract with European clubs. Mexico is coming off a shocking 0-0 draw with Trinidad and Tobago, but barring a meltdown of epic proportions, El Tri should still win Group A. The U.S. will play Martinique, an unranked team, tomorrow at 6:30 p.m. Group B.

articles.text: England National Team’s Marcus Rashford was the target of hatespeech online after missing a penalty kick against Italy. A mural of him in his hometown was defaced with racist messages. As the world returns back to normal with smiling faces of fans filling stadiums for their favorite sports teams, so is the cruel reality of the snarling hate and entitlement which follows. The latest issue of bad behavior follows England National Soccer team’s Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho, and Bukayo Saka, who received racist hate-mail after the three players missed their penalty kicks on Sunday in England’s 1-0 loss to Italy for the European Championship. A mural of Rashford was defaced with racist remarks in his hometown of Withington, Manchester. He used Instagram to write a heartfelt message reflecting on the kick gone wrong, and closed the long 400-word letter strongly: “I’m Marcus Rashford, 23 years old, Black man from Withington and Wythenshawe, South Manchester. If I have nothing else, I have that,” wrote Rashford, via his official Instagram. His full letter is online. A petition online to ban racist fans has already garnered 500,000 signatures, while the mural of Rashford liking has been restored. Back in the U.S., we are anywhere from being leaders in regards to ethical treatment of athletes. The current NBA season is a prime example. In Game 2 of the playoffs on May 26, a fan poured his food on Russell Westbrook as he walked to the locker room with an injury. On the same night, Atlanta Hawks’ Trae Young was spit on by a New York Knicks fan standing courtside. We saw only one group of four hikers on the one-mile trek to Alamere Falls, and just three people when hiking all the way back to the car via the same route from Wildcat Camp. articles.text: Weekly broadcasts available online now Aurora Theatre, in its weekly online broadcast “Aurora Connects,” invited California Shakespeare Theater Artistic Director Eric Ting and Yerba Buena Center for the Arts (YBCA) CEO Deborah Cullinan last week to discuss Universal Basic Income (UBI). “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s bi-weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” Each episode is hosted by theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. articles.text: Diego Rivera’s massive mural, “Pan American Unity”, arrived at its new home, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on June 28. It will be on display on the first floor of the Roberts Family Gallery for two years, through summer 2023. On June 17, Rivera’s colossal “Pan American Unity” fresco was carefully moved from San Francisco’s City College to SFMOMA. The priceless 4,000-pound work, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster is 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 steel-framed panels bolted together and weighing 21 tons. It was designed to be portable and was moved to the college campus from Treasure Island after the conclusion of the World’s Fair, formally known as the Golden Gate International Exposition. It is the largest of the artists’ works and had completely spanned the lobby of the Diego Rivera Theater at City College. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. To learn more and for tickets, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pan-american-unity/.
articles.title: Diego Rivera’s giant mural on display at SFMOMA for 2 years

articles.text: San Francisco’s de Young Museum is presenting a new installation by renowned artist Hung Liu. The exhibition entitled “Hung Liu: Golden Gate,” opens this Saturday, July 17. Liu, based in Oakland, is one of the most important Chinese-born artists currently working in the United States. The exhibition combs through new and existing works by the artist, who highlights international and domestic narratives of migration. The installation reimagines some of her most iconic paintings as seen through the eyes of a Chinese-born artist. The exhibit’s central feature is a massive reinvention of Liu’s painting “Resident Alien,” (1988), on permanent display on the main Artist Hung Liu wall in the Wilsey Court at the museum. The new exhibition will be on display through March 13, 2022. The museum requires timed tickets for every visitor, including general admission. To ensure a preferred time slot, reserve tickets in advance online. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. To obtain tickets, visit: https:// deyoung.famsf.org/exhibitions/ hung-liu.

articles.text: Coloratura soprano Lila Khazoum and pianist Alexander Katzman performed a wonderful wide-ranging program of music as part of Festival Opera’s ongoing concerts at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The world of music is a very interesting place, and sometimes it is incongruous. For example, a list of the greatest pianists of all time contains the usual suspects. You might start with Johann Sebastian Bach and then include Franz Liszt and continue with Rachmaninoff and Horowitz. Those are the obvious choices. But let’s keep an open mind. Should we limit the names entirely to classical musicians? One list of great pianists includes two jazz greats Art Tatum and Oscar Peterson. I was OK with Art Tatum because Horowitz admired him. But when I saw the name Oscar Peterson, I thought his inclusion was incongruous. I said to myself… Don’t jump to conclusions. When I investigated the artistry of Oscar Peterson, I was amazed. Jazz pianists often have the technique of the greatest classical players and in addition they are able to create brilliant interpretations on the spot. Keeping this philosophy in mind, my wife and I went to the Piedmont Piano Company on Thursday evening to hear a solo piano concert by the jazz pianist Tamir Hendelman. As soon as Hendelman began to play, his opening chords served as an introduction which drew his audience in. In classical music the opening chords are often called “sit down chords“. The effect here was exactly the same. A classic jazz ensemble is usually made up of a piano, a string bass, and drums. If you closed your eyes, you could just imagine that Hendelman was an entire trio all by himself. The marvel of it all is that he makes it look so easy. And therein lies the secret of true virtuosity – making the difficult appear easy. Hendelman has a very simple stage demeanor. There is no mugging for the audience. He is there to provide music. And the music that issues forth from his piano is wondrous. Every aspect of technique is put to the service of music. He juxtaposes dynamics from the super-soft to the grandiose. Everything is kept in perfect balance. And then to make things even more interesting, he adds zesty accents. And all the while he keeps the audience guessing. Only at the end of each set did he tell us what we had heard. Things like this are completely foreign to today’s classical players. articles.text: Julia Garner stars in The Assistant. The Assistant is an extraordinary film, spare, understated, mundane in the extreme, all in the service of an abiding sense of workplace dread, possessing a grim intentionality. And yet it is strangely compelling. The narrative begins as Jane (Julia Garner) is being driven in pre-dawn darkness to her job at a movie production company in the Tribeca neighborhood of Manhattan. She is the just-hired office factotum – first in each morning, last out each evening – her title being a bottom of the totem pole production assistant to a movie-entertainment production honcho. Arriving, she enters the dark interior of office cubicles, and begins her 12-hour day by turning on the lights, brewing coffee, cleaning up her boss’ office (finding an earring near the couch), and wiping off remnants of whatever is on his desk and chair. She quickly moves on to the copy machine, running handouts of the day’s schedule, countless audition headshots of young actresses, washing dishes, answering emails, all while the company denizens begin to drift in and the phones start to ring. Packages soon arrive, are signed for, opened, reservations made for an upcoming L.A. trip. A stark, oppressiveness permeates even the commons room. People, mostly men in suits, file by, going in an out of meetings. The atmosphere seems joyless, brittle, and if Jane smiles it seems an effort, her lips a thin compressed line that tilts toward grim. Her boss, a constant presence (even when he’s gone), is only a voice behind a closed door, a harsh, abusive voice on her intra-office phone, berating her for how she handled his wife’s recent phone call. Jane knows her to be a short-tempered, suspicious woman who insists on this recent call that Jane tell her where her husband is and disbelieves her when told that Jane doesn’t “have him” at the moment. Just after mid-day, a young woman arrives who is slated to begin working as the newest assistant hire (Kristine Froseth). Jane is told to take her by car to a mid-town upscale hotel. And it’s on the ride over that she learns that the newbie was a waitress in Idaho and has no background in film production. Jane is, of course, aware that this eager, hopeful film producer is not the first to arrive at her desk, waiting to hear, “send her in.” Jane knows what awaits the Idaho waitress and is conflicted. She finally decides to share her concern with the Human Resources officer, Mr. Wilcock (Matthew Macfayden), and makes an appointment to ask for advice. Finding herself seated in front of his desk, she seems all but paralyzed by what she is there to disclose. This is a remarkable scene, and the only transactional moment in the film. Jane, haltingly, expresses her concern for the new assistant. Wilcock feigns surprise and confusion, pressing Jane for details that he finds all but imaginary. He casually points out that there are 400 people who would love her job, and does she really want to file a complaint? Jane, her helplessness palpable, finally gets up to leave. As she stands at the door, Wilcock says to her, “Don’t worry, you’re not his type.” It’s a chilling moment. Her boss is a predator, and all who work for him are enablers and complicit. The fulcrum for The Assistant is the #MeToo movement, and the faceless mogul, ensconced behind the executive suite door, is Harvey Weinstein or Roger Ailes. But unlike the movie Bombshell, there is no pushback in The Assistant. All Jane can do, if she wants to keep her much-coveted job, is remain silent. She is reminded in conversations with her parents over the phone, how fortunate she is to have found her dream job. The embedded truth is that her dream is actually a nightmare in which she is asked how much she is capable of internalizing, how much she is willing to compromise for a position that she knows is demeaning and toxic. She feels trapped by her own career objectives (she too wants to be a producer), as if trapped in a kind of panic room, surrounded by blank faces and an amorphous evil comprised of a hundred small, daily tasks. I am aware that those who search out The Assistant may wonder what it was they just viewed. It’s not really a story, but a harrowing snapshot. My hope is that its inherent power will not be quickly discarded. The Assistant. Directed by Kitty Green. Starring Julia Garner, Matthew Macfayden, Makenzie Leigh. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Director Martin Scorsese’s epic 3.5 hour mob procedural film, The Irishman, is framed by violence and ultimately betrayal. It is the story of Frank Sheeran (Robert De Niro) and his journey from truck driver to factotum to Jimmy Hoffa. As a bodyguard, fixer and consigliere, he was also a man who “paints houses” (mob code for executing someone). The film is based on the 2004 biography of Sheeran, written by Charles Brandt, and titled I Heard You Paint Houses. The story begins with a long tracking shot of an empty hallway in a rest home. The Five Satins are singing In the Still of the Night. It’s a stand-alone moment. Finally, we enter a private room and linger on an old man, white haired, anchored to a wheelchair, talking to someone off camera. He is telling his story, seen through flashbacks and explained through voiceover, that begins in the early 1950s when Frank drove a truck filled with slabs of meat, making deliveries to butchers and restaurants. One day, forced to stop due to engine trouble, peering under the truck’s hood, an older man approaches and gives him a hand to solve the problem. Unbeknownst to Frank, the benign-seeming guy, Russ Bufalino (Joe Pesci), is a notorious Philadelphia mob boss. It’s only later that the two meet again, and it’s Bufalino who introduces Frank to Jimmy Hoffa (Al Pacino), head of the powerful Teamsters Union. It proves to be a connection that will alter the course of their lives. The film again shifts to a flashback that will give structure to the rest of the film. We see Russ and Frank, now years older, about to take a road trip with their wives from Kingston, Philadelphia, to Detroit. And it’s that journey, with a number of pit stops along the way, so the women can smoke, that gives Russ and Frank the opportunity to reminisce. Each stop on the three-day journey is comprised of a lengthy vignette that illustrates not only the evolution of their friendship, but of Frank’s abiding closeness with Hoffa, to include his importance to keeping in place the union-mob alliance. The union loaned the wise guys money from their pension fund for whatever, and the mob provided intimidation (maybe a house painted) when necessary. As Frank shares his story, on occasion seated in a wheelchair, clearly a man alone, we are told that he had a wife and four daughters. But from the beginning, it’s clear that he has chosen not his family but the mob. He has given himself entirely over to these men who are, to a fault, lethally Machiavellian. He embraces the illusion that this criminal clan represents familial loyalty, which transcends even those of his own family. It’s a brotherhood to which he gives an unwavering, stoic commitment. Never does he understand that this meta-family is an illusion and is devoid of anything resembling devotion. What drives these men are power, obedience to a code, and money. They live by an understood silence, regardless of outcomes (never name names) and are masters of constructing euphemisms when discussing a job, their spare dialogue always filled with the implied, however tortured, never the explicit. As we witness Frank in that senior care facility, on occasion slipping into regret, knowing that those who wanted to care about him in the past are now absent, it is now clear that the emotional bankruptcy of his life has resulted in his final days spent speaking to strangers (or the F.B.I.). Everyone is gone, some killed, others dying in prison, his daughters in the wind. There are two things I find interesting about Martin Scorsese as a filmmaker. He so often has chosen a dark pallet to examine the human condition, from his early film Mean Streets, and now to The Irishman. His stories inhabit a nihilistic, violent world that is a place apart, the characters driven by forces seemingly outside them, unhampered by even a hint of self-reflection. Nothing seems to give any of them pause. I also wonder why, in his movies, there are so few women. Women represent family, a bond, a promise, and it is they who are abandoned, or relegated to a world that seems tangential to the band of mob brothers whose connections represent a chain that can, in truth, be broken without remorse. Ultimately, it’s just business. Finally, two things: The Irishman is beautifully acted, with layers of fine performances, all resembling, in the aggregate, a Scorsese acting troupe. If you are a cinephile and have followed the astonishing career of this fine director, now in his 70s, don’t miss this film. While long, it never wavers or slows, its chronological pace inexorable while telling a story that is eminently accessible. The Irishman. Directed by Martin Scorsese. Starring Robert DeNiro, Al Pacino, Joe Pesci. 3 hrs, 29 min. Rated R

articles.text: Ben Whishaw provides the voice of Paddington. Review by Chris Honoré Paddington is a dazzling live action/CGI animated take on Michal Brand’s classic children’s books, a feature film that feels both old-fashion as well as hightech. It’s also an origin story that is funny, charming and sprinkled with puns. We first meet Paddington (Ben Whishaw), living with his aunt and uncle (Imelda Stauton and veteran French actor Michal Gambon). Years earlier, we’re told, a British explorer had discovered in “Darkest Peru” the existence of talking bears and goes about teaching them all things British, including English and a love of marmalade. Paddington’s aunt decides that the time has come for Paddington to make his way in the world, and it’s decided that the most hospitable place for him will be London where bears of his ilk are welcomed. So off he goes, wearing his familiar red floppy hat (that belonged to the explorer), and carrying enough food for the long boat ride to England. Eventually he arrives and makes his way to Paddington Station with his battered suitcase. It is there that he discovers that Londoners are not surprised at a walking, talking bear, but are also generally rude and unhelpful – until Paddington meets the Brown family. Mrs. Brown (Sally Hawkins) who shows the homeless traveler some kindness and sympathy and names him after the station where they found him. Meanwhile, the other Browns – Mr. Brown (Hugh Bonneville), daughter Judy (Madeline Harris), and son Jonathan (Samuel Joslin) – while intrigued, are somewhat skeptical. Especially Mr. Brown. Having found a home, though a bit homesick, Paddington gradually settles into London life. There are a few amusing antics along the way, but he eventually finds his stride and regains his confident pluck. Meanwhile, a local museum taxidermist, Millicent Clyde (Nicole Kidman), learns of Paddington’s existence and is determined to track him down, kidnap him, stuff him, and, of course, add him to her museum collection. And thus begins a number of chase scenes, stand-offs, and narrow escapes by Paddington. There’s never a dull moment, and it’s all pure fun. Plus, the visuals are superb, tactile, inventive. The bear’s facial features are remarkable, allowing the young audience to make a strong connection with him. Which they do throughout this nicely told, engaging story. Paddington. Live actionCGI animation. Directed by Paul King. With voices of Ben Whishaw, Sally Hawkins and Nicole Kidman. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Planes is the zippy, family-friendly story of a courageous little rural crop-duster called Dusty (Dane Cook) who dreams of flying higher and faster and yearns to enter an international air race called the Wings Around the Globe. The problem is that he is built to fly low and slow, his one prop taking him over stretching farm fields, mere feet above the ground. Plus, there’s an added complication: Dusty has a fear of heights. His friends, like Dottie a forklift (Terri Hatcher), and Chug, a fuel truck ((Brad Garrett), encourage Dusty to follow his dream. Chug even gives him a book titled Air Racing for Dummies. Improbably, Dusty enters the air race trials and qualifies in the top five. But he realizes that his tenacity and skills are not enough, and he searches for a mentor and coach. He turns to Skipper (Stacy Keach), a crusty old WWII Navy plane. Of course, the old air dog knows that Dusty needs to up his game and his speed and he’ll have to practice those ballet-like twists and turns. Skipper also instills in him a can-do spirit. Dusty finally tells Skipper he is afraid of heights. But Skipper’s motto is “Volo Pro Veritas” (I fly for truth). Yep, a little Latin never hurts a Disney story. So the little guy shows up for the race with a healthy dose of trepidation and meets, for the first time, his (gulp) international competition: Ripsinger (Robert Craig Smith), Ishani (Priyanka Chopra), British Bulldog (John Cleese), The Mexican Chupacabra (Carlos Alazraqui), and Rochelle (Julia Louis-Dreyfus). All are champions in their respective countries, and since this is a ‘round the globe race, there is some great scenery. Each leg of the race offers a different challenge, each is exciting, with noisy swoops and wing-tipping close calls as the planes buzz around the course. Youngsters will love it. Of course, though some of the racers are not above stretching the rules a bit, Dusty never compromises his integrity and holds to the rules and his sense of good sportsmanship. Planes. Directed by Klay Hall. Disney. With the voices of Dane Cook, Stacy Keach, Brad Garrett. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG. A scene from Disney’s Planes.

articles.text: West Edge Opera will perform this summer at Bruns Amphitheater in Orinda. West Edge Opera will perform three operas at the open-air Bruns Amphitheater from July 24 through August 8 as part of its West Edge Festival. articles.text: Though Monday, July 5 was an extension of the July 4 holiday this year, the First Mondays Reading Group had a solid turnout of 11 readers calling in for the Zoom gathering. The participants were: Sarah Johnson, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Alicia Rivera, Karin Fetherston, Laura Goldman, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Melba Yee had suggested Interior Chinatown by Charles Yu for the July discussion. It is a 2020 novel that received broad critical acclaim. Among other honors, it won the 2020 National Book Award for Fiction. Yu uses the unusual structure of a screenplay to tell the story of Willis Wu, the “Generic Asian Man.” It is also the story of his Chinatown, the Golden Palace restaurant, which Wu lives above, and the racism he and others endure. The restaurant is the setting for a fictional, constantly in production police film show, “Black and White.” Wu sometimes gets to be “Background Oriental Making a Weird Face,” or “Disgraced Son,” and occasionally “Delivery Guy” in the film. He longs to be the “Kung Fu Guy,” the pinnacle Asian male on screens worldwide, but he only gets small roles. Through Wu, Yu explores Hollywood’s and our country’s constant use of clichés and stereotypes about Asians and Asian-Americans . The group of readers was split on their reaction to the book. The majority of readers were enthusiastic about the book, but others had issues with it. The readers appreciated the author’s creative approach to address a real problem that confronts Asian Americans, and what it means to live in a country that views race as a primary identification of people. They liked that the book focused on the stereotypes of Asian Americans. When some Asian American readers were growing up, Asian American were perceived as the model minority, but for the most part they were invisible. In some parts of the country, there were few Asian Americans. The group recognized that Yu’s writing style and format for the book are different and creative. The readers enjoyed that Yu made them more aware of discriminatory perceptions and attitudes that some had not been fully conscious of. Yu sometimes presents these stereotypes with dark humor that may cause a wry laugh, but they are sadly very real and hurtful. What is happening in the Interior Chinatown screenplay is also happening in real life today. Interior Chinatown was a catalyst for the group members to discuss the meaning of “home” for immigrants and their decedents, the country’s racial history, their own personal experiences with racism, and how they acted and protected themselves from it. Asian Americans often kept to themselves and tried not to “make trouble.” However, with recent, more visible violent acts against Asians and the emergence of the Anti-Hate movement, speaking up now and addressing what has happened was seen as important and overdue. For some members of the group this was deeply touching, as the Asian experience is also our society’s human experience. Much of our country’s social justice movement has focused on our country’s treatment of African-Americans, but generating an awareness of, and focus on, Asian stereotypes is an important contribution by Yu. These attitudes and tropes have resulted in hateful, violent acts towards Asians both in the past and the present. While the group recognized the value of Interior Chinatown some readers had problems with the book’s structure and Yu’s writing style. They found it confusing and had trouble making a distinction between Willis Wu’s real life and his acting life. Some readers found it difficult to connect with the Wu character. It seemed there was a gender divide with the women readers enjoying the book more than the men. The group previously selected The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, Deacon King Kong by James McBride, and Nomadland by Jessica Bruder for August, September, and October respectively. The group will meet next on Monday, August 2, at 1:30 p.m. outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New members are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Registration is required by contacting John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: The openings in a building, principally doors and windows, are what architects refer to as fenestration. The sizes, composition, and detailing of the openings are one of the most important design considerations in determining the style and quality of the architecture. Like so much in this field, this issue is a mixture and balance between aesthetics and function, heavily influenced by building code requirements. There are of course various types of window operations, such as casement, double hung, tilt and turn, as well as fixed windows (non-operable). But the choice is not only how they open, but also how well they are visually suited to the architectural style of the building – something that, as we have mentioned before, is always evolving and changing. The early high-rise buildings in the late 1800’s were equipped, for example, with residential style double Photos by Will Adams Good window fenestration requires detailing that coordinates operation, size, shape, and how the windows fit into the walls of the building, all the while making sure it looks good. Other openings in the building can also be considered fenestration. The trick is to give equal design consideration to all utilitarian components of a building -- such as this louver located in its own dormer. (Note the roof slope nomenclature discussed in the last column: 12:12 main roof & 6:12 dormer roof.) Fenestration includes the exterior composition of all the doors and windows together. The asymmetrical arrangement of the numerous openings in this Piedmont Mediterranean style home is interesting, rich in texture, and quite wonderful! articles.text: Joe Sullivan, loving husband, father, son, brother, brother-inlaw, cousin, uncle, godfather, and friend, experienced a fatal heart attack on March 1, 2020. Born Joseph Michael Sullivan II on August 12, 1956 in Ann Arbor, Michigan, Joe was the son of William and Helen Sullivan. He effortlessly became a lifetime Wolverine fan as his father finished his doctoral degree in pharmacy at the University of Michigan. Joe’s family relocated to Oakland, where he was raised and attended Corpus Christi School. He excelled in sports at Piedmont High School, where he was a member of the football and track teams. In addition, he learned to serve his community at a young age and carried his passion for helping others throughout his entire life. As a Boy Scout, he achieved the Order of the Arrow and he developed his love for the outdoors, especially camping and rafting. On June 5, 1982, Joe married his high school sweetheart, Carol Lee Robinson, at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont. Together they built a loving family. In October 1986, they became the proud parents of Ryan Sullivan. Joe and Ryan shared many interests, especially playing football, watching and talking sports, and outdoor activities. Joe served as a loyal volunteer to Boy Scouts Troop 6 and especially loved to go on the camp outings. Joe owned and operated the Book Tree, an independent bookstore associated with their family business, Sullivan’s Montclair Pharmacy. For 50 years the Sullivan businesses were a fixture in Montclair Village, known for personal service. Joe served his community as the President of the Oakland-Montclair Lions Club. Joe’s loyal commitment to organizations benefiting others made him an outstanding memJoe Sullivan, the son of Bill and Helen Sullivan, died last year from a fatal heart attack on March 1, 2020. ber of many groups. He joined the Grizzly Riders, an association providing student scholarships and financial support at the University of Montana. Joe continued to dedicate his time by becoming a Volunteer Firefighter in Auburn, California. He thrived in this role with his love for barbecue and response to action. articles.text: Taking a close look at the entirety of St. James Drive The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group tries to walk all Piedmont streets during the year. Last Wednesday morning, July 7, they decided that it would it a good day to tackle a long walk. A strong turnout of 27 walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra, and they ready for a long, mostly flat walk down and back the .8 mile length of St. James Drive. On hand were: Brenda Ferrero, Sherry Jacobs, Susan Field, Albert Chen, Swee Ling Chen, Haybert Houston, Nancy Olsen, Charlene Louie, Mark Greenberg, Andre Greenberg, Melba Yee, Dave DeRoche, Stella Houston, Priscilla Wanerus, Phil Witte, Adrienne Hamlin, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Alicia Rivera, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Cat Gustafson, Alan Goldhammer, Bob Gustafson, Sarah Johnson, Jim Kuo, and Dick Carter. One of the last walks the group had before Covid restrictions In March 2020 was on St. James, so there was some added pleasure to be able to walk as a group on the street again. In November 2019 the walkers visited Cavendish Lane to see the repair of the block-long hillside street after it was undermined. It is a half block from where St. James ends at Park Blvd., so the walkers added it to their planned excursion. Due to the large number of walkers, it looked more like a parade down Highland Avenue to Sheridan and Wildwood, along the Hall Fenway to Crocker and Hampton Avenues. Along the way they enjoyed the fragrant, flowering jasmine plants and especially what was almost like a field of them in a Hampton Avenue yard. The group walked to the corner of St. James and La Salle Avenue, where two tall columns mark the entrance in the early 1900s to St. James Woods, part of the Upper Piedmont Estates neighborhood development. Originally there were lights on top of these columns, but they were removed at some point. The St. James’ homeowners later asked the City to install new light fixtures, but the cost exceeded the City’s budget. Post cartoonist and Wednesday walker Phil Witte lives on St. James and told the group about the street. The homes were built over time during the first half of the 20th century by different builders, so the architectural styles are varied. The sidewalks on both sides of the street the length of St. James have a distinctive tile design. The group enjoyed the long, winding street and appreciated the old streetlights, a very old cactus with a very large trunk, a curious dragon wood sculpture that guards one home, and other wonderful homes and gardens. The walkers also saw two pedestrian stairways, one that climbs up to Cambrian Avenue and the other that leads to Sandringham Road. A little further on, they also saw the top of another set of stairs that goes down to Trestle Glen Road The walkers finally made it to the end of St. James where Corpus Christi Church stands at Park Blvd. It had been a long walk, but the group was still up for a walk several hundred feet to Cavendish Lane to see its condition. This is a narrow street, truly a lane, which was damaged in February 2017 after it was undermined by heavy rains and a Trestle Glen neighbor’s home construction project below. This an Oakland street, but there are four Piedmont homeowners at its end. They were unable to access their homes by car for six weeks. The City of Piedmont took action to make temporary repairs until a permanent fix was made, which turned out to be two and a half years later in October 2019. They went up the lane and though the roadway was gully repaired, they were surprised to see that the area below the street still looks like a construction zone. The walkers were glad this situation was not in their backyards. Some members of this energetic group wanted to go down Trestle Glen, find the stairs that lead up to St. James and climb them, which is exactly what they did. Once back on St. James they retraced their many steps back to the Exedra. It had been well over four miles and a twohour walk. However, everyone seemed to enjoy the extra walking and talking with their walking friends. The Walking on Wednesday group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required with John Wilk at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

Obituary Joe Sullivan dies on March 1, 2020 Joe Sullivan, loving husband, father, son, brother, brother-inlaw, cousin, uncle, godfather, and friend, experienced a fatal heart attack on March 1, 2020. Born Joseph Michael Sullivan II on August 12, 1956 in Ann Arbor, Michigan, Joe was the son of William and Helen Sullivan. He effortlessly became a lifetime Wolverine fan as his father finished his doctoral degree in pharmacy at the University of Michigan. Joe’s family relocated to Oakland, where he was raised and attended Corpus Christi School. He excelled in sports at Piedmont High School, where he was a member of the football and track teams. In addition, he learned to serve his community at a young age and carried his passion for helping others throughout his entire life. As a Boy Scout, he achieved the Order of the Arrow and he developed his love for the outdoors, especially camping and rafting. On June 5, 1982, Joe married his high school sweetheart, Carol Lee Robinson, at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont. Together they built a loving family. In October 1986, they became the proud parents of Ryan Sullivan. Joe and Ryan shared many interests, especially playing football, watching and talking sports, and outdoor activities. Joe served as a loyal volunteer to Boy Scouts Troop 6 and especially loved to go on the camp outings. Joe owned and operated the Book Tree, an independent bookstore associated with their family business, Sullivan’s Montclair Pharmacy. For 50 years the Sullivan businesses were a fixture in Montclair Village, known for personal service. Joe served his community as the President of the Oakland-Montclair Lions Club. They include the familiar double (or even triple) glazing, and low E glass coatings. I have found that one of the most difficult parts of building design is to make the overall exterior composition of the fenestration jibe with the requirements of the interior rooms. In other words, the fenestration has to work both inside and out, visually and functionally. In addition to considering the proportions and light and ventilation of each interior room, certain windows (in bedrooms) have to be sized to meet emergency exit requirements to allow occupants escape and firefighters egress. Another important building code requirement that enters into fenestration design is the requirement for tempered glass. Tempered glass is stronger, but more importantly, breaks into small granular chunks instead of dangerous dagger-like shards, as does normal glass. All glass in doors, and windows adjacent to doors, is now required to be tempered glass.
